title: Hip Pain: Groin Pain, Outer Hip Pain and When It Is Arthritis
metaDescription: Groin pain often points to the hip joint, outer hip pain to nearby tendons. Learn the causes, warning signs and a stepwise approach to treatment.
intro: Pain in the groin, the front of the thigh or the knee usually points to a problem inside the hip joint, and arthritis is a common reason. Pain on the outer side of the hip or in the buttock more often comes from the tendons around the hip, or from the back. A doctor's examination, and sometimes an X-ray, is needed to tell them apart.

sections.heading: Where you feel hip pain matters
sections.body: The place of pain gives a useful clue. Groin pain, or pain in the front of the thigh or knee, usually suggests the hip joint itself. Pain on the outer hip or buttock often comes from the soft tissues around the joint. Knee pain can sometimes be the only sign of a hip problem, and back problems can also cause pain in the buttock, outer hip or down the leg.

sections.heading: What does hip arthritis feel like?
sections.body: Hip arthritis (osteoarthritis, where the smooth lining of the joint wears down) is most often felt in the groin, though it can be in the thigh and may spread to the buttock or knee. Common signs are:
bullets: Pain and stiffness that are worse in the morning or after sitting
Pain when bending the hip, for example on stairs or when putting on socks
Less movement in the hip and sometimes a limp
A grinding feeling, and in time pain at rest or at night

sections.heading: What causes pain on the outer side of the hip?
sections.body: Outer hip pain is often linked to the muscles and tendons over the bony point of the hip. The older name is trochanteric bursitis (inflammation of a fluid-filled cushion over the bone), and it is now also linked to gluteal tendinopathy (a sore tendon from the buttock muscles). It is common, can spread down the leg and often affects both hips. Overdoing exercise can also strain these tissues, and this often settles within a few days.

sections.heading: How is the cause found?
sections.body: Your doctor asks about your symptoms and past health, then examines your hip. They check tenderness, movement, grinding and how you walk. An X-ray is the main scan and can show a narrowed joint space and bony changes. An MRI or CT scan is used only occasionally, so most people do not need one.

sections.heading: What is our usual approach to treatment?
sections.body: Treatment is tailored to you, and we go step by step. This is our usual approach, not a fixed rule:
bullets: Medicines first, such as paracetamol or anti-inflammatory tablets, chosen to suit you. Do not use over-the-counter painkillers for more than two weeks without speaking to a doctor.
Once pain eases, gentle exercise and strengthening, built up gradually. Walking or swimming help general fitness, and losing weight eases strain if you are overweight.

If that is not enough, physiotherapy treatments such as ultrasound or short-wave, used for pain relief only. Evidence is modest: a Cochrane review found weak evidence of pain relief from ultrasound, in knee arthritis, with no hip studies.
An injection only for selected patients, for pain relief. Steroid injections are used for conditions such as bursitis.
Surgery last, and only if it is appropriate.

sections.heading: Does hip arthritis always need surgery?
sections.body: No. Surgery is usually considered only when arthritis pain causes disability and does not improve with non-surgical treatment. Hip replacement is the most common operation. We explain the options, benefits and risks, and the decision is yours.

sections.heading: When should I see a doctor quickly?
sections.body: Get prompt assessment if you have fallen or injured your hip, or if the pain is very bad or worsening. Also seek help if you cannot walk or manage stairs, feel feverish or unwell, or have lost weight without trying. See a doctor too if pain has not improved after two weeks of regular painkillers.

faqs.q: Is groin pain always a hip problem?
faqs.a: No. Groin pain usually suggests the hip joint, but hernias, swollen glands and gynaecological problems can also cause it. An examination sorts this out.

faqs.q: Can a back problem cause hip pain?
faqs.a: Yes. Back problems can cause pain in the buttock, outer hip or leg. Knee pain can also be the only sign of a hip problem.

faqs.q: Do I need an X-ray for hip pain?
faqs.a: Often yes if arthritis is suspected, because X-rays are the main test. They show joint narrowing and bony changes. MRI or CT is only occasionally needed.

faqs.q: Will exercise make hip arthritis worse?
faqs.a: Gentle, graded exercise is advised once pain has eased. Low-impact activities such as swimming or cycling are usually easier on the joint than stair climbing. Ask your doctor or physiotherapist what suits you.

faqs.q: Do hip injections and ultrasound help?
faqs.a: Steroid injections may give pain relief in selected people. Ultrasound has only weak evidence, and the review we read looked at knees, not hips.
